newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil coffee supply problems fail to materialize.
newsitem.headline: Brazil coffee supply problems fail to materialize.

text.p: So is there enough coffee in Brazil?
Few people six months ago would have expected at the start of April to see forecasts of another high month of exports, with March figures still unclosed at 1.41 million 60-kg bags.
Few people would have expected to see a government auction of just over 300,000 bags to the coffee sector with sales of less than 40 percent.
So is the anticipated squeeze in the inter-harvest period still going to happen?
"We thought that in March we would have already started to see a shortage," said Nathan Herszkowicz, president of the Sao Paulo Coffee Industry Union.
"Perhaps it will now happen at the end of April, perhaps in May. Perhaps it won't happen at all if the new harvest starts to come in early," he added.
In January, the union, working with a 27 million-bag crop in 1996/97, anticipated there would a supply shortfall of 2.7 million bags which would have to met by government auctions.
Now however the deficit is seen to be a lot smaller, Herszkowicz said.
The poor level of sales in this week's auction was said to have helped weigh on sentiment in the New York futures market which ended sharply lower yesterday amid fund-selling.
Roaster representatives blamed too high opening prices and difficulty in obtaining credit lines as the main reasons for the lack of interest.
But there is also the fact domestic roasters are not meeting any problems in finding coffee in the domestic market.
"The problem is not supply but price," said David Nahum, secretary-general of the Brazilian Coffee Industry Association (ABIC) which represents roasters.
Some traders say one other possible reason for the low sales is that internal consumption is not running as expected at 900,000 bags a month.
Or that coffee sold in auctions to the soluble industry at nuch lower prices is finding its way back to the domestic roasting industry.
Meanwhile exports continue unabated.
Back in November last year, analysts were anticipating shipments of around one million bags a month in January to March would leave virtually nothing for the second quarter of 1997.

Shipments each month this quarter have exceeded one million bags and yet registrations for April as of March 21 were already 1.40 million bags while a further 659,335 million bags had been registered for May.

Until now the "unexpected" supply is believed to have come from private producer stocks of previous harvests. But these are thought to have reached their peak and producer sales in March were lower than in February, said Manoel Bertone, vice-president of the National Coffee Council which represents growers.
The key now is whether producers will look to anticipate the 1997/98 harvest in a bid to take advantage of the higher prices.
Crop maturation in some lower-lying areas is said to be quite advanced which could see early harvesting in May.
But regardless of the condition of the crop, the key is price, traders said.
"What experience has taught us is what anticipates the crop is not the weather but prices," one dealer said.
One trader estimates that around eight percent of the harvest could be brought in in April, May and June, with 100,000 bags this month, 500,000 bags in May and 1.5 million in June.
Is that enough to tide the market over?
"I think conillons and Group IIs will probably make it. But Group Is which will really only be available in August, I think there may be some problems," he said.
((-Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 5074151))
